![The 7B Conductor (leftmost, solid bars) tops GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek R1, and Claude Opus 4 on both GPQA-Diamond and LiveCodeBench, despite being far smaller than any of the models it coordinates. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

In *Learning to Orchestrate Agents in Natural Language with the Conductor* [[1]](#ref-1) (ICLR 2026), [Stefan Nielsen](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2396336821), [Edoardo Cetin](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2326294214), [Peter Schwendeman](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2396352279), [Qi Sun](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2326487319), [Jinglue Xu](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2397339171), and [Yujin Tang](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2326422916) (Sakana AI, University of Michigan, and Institute of Science Tokyo) train a 7B *conductor* with reinforcement learning to plan how a pool of LLMs should talk to each other and what to tell each one, and then let it call itself recursively to spend more compute on hard queries.

> Powerful large language models (LLMs) from different providers have been expensively trained and finetuned to specialize across varying domains. In this work, we introduce *a new kind of Conductor model trained with reinforcement learning* to automatically discover powerful coordination strategies among LLMs. Our Conductor learns not only to *design targeted communication topologies for effective agent-to-agent collaboration, but also to prompt engineer focused instructions* to the LLMs to maximally leverage their individual capabilities. We show that, by learning optimal coordination strategies over pools of powerful worker LLMs, *a 7B Conductor achieves significant performance gains beyond any individual worker, attaining state-of-the-art results in challenging reasoning benchmarks*, such as LiveCodeBench and GPQA. By training with randomized agent pools, our conductor effectively adapts to arbitrary sets of open- and closed-source agents, meeting any user requirements. Furthermore, allowing the Conductor to select itself as a worker gives rise to *recursive topologies, elevating performance with a new form of dynamic test-time scaling* through online iterative adaptation. More broadly, ours is among the early work demonstrating *language model coordination can be unlocked through RL*, where powerful coordination strategies emerge naturally in LLMs through pure end-to-end reward maximization.

## Methods

The Conductor is itself an LLM, a 7B model finetuned from a Qwen2.5-Coder checkpoint [[2]](#ref-2), with no architectural change to the transformer. The novelty is not the model but what it is trained to *output*: instead of answering a query, it emits a *complete agentic workflow in natural language*, which an outer loop then executes by calling the worker models.

### What the Conductor outputs

- **The output is a parsed workflow.** After its chain-of-thought, the Conductor emits up to five workflow steps as three aligned Python lists: the natural-language subtask for each step, the integer id of the worker assigned to it, and an *access list* naming which earlier steps' outputs that worker may see. The harness parses these lists and runs the steps in order, prompting each named worker with its subtask plus only the prior responses its access list grants. The Conductor produces no answer content of its own.
- **Natural language as the output medium is the design choice.** Prior multi-agent routers pick from a set of pre-specified topologies. Emitting the workflow as free-form text instead gives what the authors call complete specification freedom, letting one model express best-of-N, sequential chains, or arbitrary parallel trees within the same format. Both halves of an agentic step, which worker to call and what exact instruction it gets, are learned jointly, so the Conductor does prompt engineering rather than only routing.

![The Conductor's output for a coding problem: a short plan, then three aligned lists, the per-step subtasks, the worker `model_id` assigned to each, and the `access_list` controlling what each worker sees. Here worker 2 designs an algorithm and worker 0 implements it in Python with worker 2's output in context. Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure2.png){fig-align="center"}

### How it is trained

- **End-to-end with GRPO on the executed workflow's reward.** Training uses GRPO [[3]](#ref-3) with a two-part reward: 0 if the three lists can't be parsed, then 1 if the *executed* workflow's final output matches the ground-truth solution and 0.5 otherwise. The signal comes only from running the whole plan to completion, with no supervised labels for who-should-do-what. From that single reward the authors observe problem breakdowns, worker-matched instructions, and communication topologies emerge on their own.
- **The training set is 960 deliberately-hard problems.** The Conductor trains on 960 problems across four domains: MATH500 [[4]](#ref-4) (math), MMLU [[5]](#ref-5) (multitask knowledge), LiveCodeBench [[6]](#ref-6) (code), and RLPR [[7]](#ref-7) (general reasoning). The authors pick the harder variants of benchmarks common in multi-agent work, using AIME-style difficulty over GSM8K [[8]](#ref-8) and pairing LiveCodeBench's oldest version for training with its newest for testing, which guards against contamination.
- **Randomized agent pools during training.** The available worker set is resampled at each training step, so the Conductor learns to coordinate arbitrary mixes of open and closed models rather than memorizing one fixed roster. At test time a user can hand it any pool, including one with no paid API calls.

### Recursion at test time

- **Recursive self-calls buy more test-time compute.** Letting the Conductor name itself as a worker produces recursive topologies: an inner call receives its parent's output together with the previous agent's response. Recursion is unlocked by a short finetune that instantiates one recursion call for half the samples in each batch, and is capped at a maximum depth. Spending more recursive depth raises accuracy on hard queries.

![Conductor schematic: the model reads a user query, then coordinates specialized workers (here Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemini, and GPT) with per-agent instructions to solve a task that mixes mathematical reasoning and translation. Figure 11 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure11.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure11-full.png"}

## Results

The Conductor is evaluated in-domain on held-out questions from its four training tasks and out-of-domain on AIME 2025 [[9]](#ref-9), BigCodeBench [[10]](#ref-10), and GPQA-Diamond [[11]](#ref-11). Baselines include the strongest single models (Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and several open models), multi-agent methods (Mixture-of-Agents [[12]](#ref-12), MASRouter [[13]](#ref-13), Smoothie [[14]](#ref-14), RouterDC [[15]](#ref-15)), and single-model self-reflection, with cost tracked as the average number of model calls per query.

### Accuracy

- **Beats each pool member alone, averaged across seven tasks.** The 7B Conductor averages 77.27 across the four in-domain and three out-of-domain tasks, ahead of GPT-5 (74.78), Gemini 2.5 Pro (70.97), and Claude Sonnet 4 (65.69), and it sets the best score on GPQA-Diamond (87.5) and LiveCodeBench (83.93) [[1]](#ref-1). These single models are the Conductor's own workers, so the comparison pits the orchestrated pool against each member run alone rather than against an outside frontier. The gain comes from routing and composing models the Conductor already has, with no added capability of its own.

![The full comparison: the 7B Conductor (bottom row) against open and closed single models across the four in-domain tasks (MATH500, MMLU, RLPR, LiveCodeBench) and three unseen tasks (AIME25, BigCodeBench, GPQA-Diamond). It posts the best seven-task average (77.27) and the top score on every column shown. Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table1.png){fig-align="center"}

![In-domain (MATH500, MMLU, RLPR, LiveCodeBench) and unseen-task accuracy: the Conductor (leftmost, bold) clears every single-model and multi-agent baseline, including 5-turn reflection agents. Figure 4 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure4.png){fig-align="center"}

### Cost efficiency

- **Beats multi-agent baselines at a fraction of the cost.** Averaged across tasks the Conductor lands above Mixture-of-Agents, Smoothie, MASRouter, and RouterDC while making far fewer calls, roughly three per query against Mixture-of-Agents' eight (Figure 5) [[1]](#ref-1).

![Performance against average number of model calls: the Conductor reaches the highest average performance at roughly three calls per query, above Mixture-of-Agents (MoA), Smoothie, and MASRouter, which cost more per query, and RouterDC, which is cheaper but far weaker. Figure 5 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure5.png){fig-align="center"}

### Scaling and adaptivity

- **The 7B's edge over the 3B is better instructions.** A 3B Conductor already learns to concentrate calls on the three strongest models, and scaling to 7B adds further gains even when the agent selection is held fixed, which the authors attribute to better-written instructions. The Conductor also matches compute to difficulty, using two agents on MMLU and three or four on LiveCodeBench.

## My Notes

- **RL works here, where Trinity's did not.** The Conductor trains a coordinator with reinforcement learning, while the sibling [Trinity](/posts/20260629-trinity-llm-coordinator/) [[16]](#ref-16) found REINFORCE too low-signal to learn from and switched to an evolutionary strategy. The split is scale and action space: the Conductor is a full 7B model emitting natural-language topologies and prompts, a rich space reward signals can shape, whereas Trinity optimized a ~10K-parameter head over a discrete pick-a-model-and-role choice. The two papers map opposite corners of the same coordinator-training problem, and Sakana ships both as separate models behind one endpoint in [Sakana Fugu](/posts/20260629-fugu-release/) [[17]](#ref-17): the quality-first Fugu-Ultra builds on the Conductor, while the everyday Fugu builds on Trinity. They are not two stages of one orchestrator.
- **Recursion beats reflection as a scaling knob.** A self-reflection loop re-runs one model on its own output. The Conductor's recursive self-call instead re-plans the whole topology with fresh instructions, and it shifts toward the strongest workers (Claude and Gemini) in deeper rounds. That makes recursion depth a compute dial the user can turn up, and it is the mechanism [Sakana Fugu](/posts/20260629-fugu-release/) [[17]](#ref-17) later exposes as its higher-effort Fugu-Ultra tier.
- **Accuracy reported per call.** Most multi-agent papers report only accuracy. The Conductor's Figure 5 puts accuracy against average model calls, and its win arrives at roughly three calls against Mixture-of-Agents' eight. This is the economy the [triager pattern](/posts/20260429-frontier-model-lower-bill/) chases from the cost side, escalating only when needed, reached here by learning when fewer agents suffice. [MAPO](/posts/20260520-adaptive-collaboration-mapo/) [[18]](#ref-18) trains a closely related decision about when to defer.
- **The pool sets the ceiling.** The single models the Conductor beats are its own workers, so the result measures the orchestrated pool against each member alone rather than against an outside frontier. The 7B adds no answer capability of its own. On AIME, where GPT-5 is already the best worker, the paper says the full-pool Conductor only matches its own GPT-5-only variant, which bounds the gain: orchestration helps when the right answer is split across different models, and reduces to picking the single best worker when one model already dominates. This is the same limit [Trinity](/posts/20260629-trinity-llm-coordinator/) [[16]](#ref-16) hits against its per-question-best oracle.

- [Sakana Fugu: One Model to Command Them All](/posts/20260629-fugu-release/): the product whose two models extend this pair separately — Fugu-Ultra builds on the Conductor (with recursion exposed as its higher tier), Fugu builds on Trinity — behind one endpoint.
- [Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies](/posts/20260430-multi-agent-system-search/): searches prompts and topologies offline, the same structure the Conductor instead learns by reinforcement learning.
- [Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs](/posts/20260520-adaptive-collaboration-mapo/): trains a deferral policy, a learned cousin of the Conductor's decision about how many agents to involve.
- [MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems](/posts/20250802-mast-multi-agent-failures/): catalogs how multi-agent pipelines break, the failure modes a learned conductor has to avoid.
